1.topic: The meaning of the death, resurrection and ascension of Jesus
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain why the death of Jesus is central to the Christian faith (Mark 10:45; Romans 5:8);
2. describe the evidence the Gospels give for the resurrection, including the story of Thomas (John 20:19-29);
3. narrate the ascension and say what the promise of Jesus' return means (Acts 1:1-11).

## Materials

Bibles, a chart of the appearances of the risen Jesus, a picture of Mount Olivet, strips of paper for the class activity.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: what would convince you that someone you knew had really come back to life? Take answers. Then say that Thomas wanted exactly that kind of proof.

## Development

1. Recall briefly the crucifixion. Read Mark 10:45 and Romans 5:6-8, and ask what Jesus' death achieved: ransom, forgiveness, reconciliation.
2. Read Mark 15:38 and discuss the tearing of the temple curtain, and the centurion's words (Mark 15:39).
3. Read John 20:19-29. Jesus appears when the doors are locked. Thomas's demand and his confession "My Lord and my God".
4. Read 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 for the list of witnesses.
5. Read Acts 1:1-11 for the ascension. Ask why the angels said "Why do you stand here looking into the sky?"

## Class activity

Each group writes on strips one piece of evidence for the resurrection and one meaning of the ascension, and pastes them on the board.

## Evaluation

1. What was Thomas's confession of faith?
2. How long did Jesus appear to the disciples before the ascension?

## Assignment

Write a short paragraph explaining why the resurrection matters more to Christians than any other event.

reading.title: Why the cross, the empty tomb and the cloud matter
reading.content:
# Why the cross, the empty tomb and the cloud matter

## The meaning of the death of Jesus

Christians do not see the cross only as a sad event. Jesus said that "the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). A **ransom** is a price paid to free someone. Paul wrote, "God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). So the death of Jesus shows God's love, brings forgiveness of sins and makes peace between God and people. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), which Christians understand to mean that the way to God is now open to all.

## Evidence for the resurrection

The Gospels and Paul give several kinds of evidence. The tomb was found empty. Different people saw Jesus alive, in different places and at different times. Paul lists Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred believers at once, James and later himself (1 Corinthians 15:5-8). Frightened disciples who had locked themselves in a room became bold preachers.

## Thomas

When Jesus first appeared to the disciples on Sunday evening, Thomas was not there. He said he would not believe unless he saw the nail marks in Jesus' hands and put his finger where the nails were. A week later Jesus appeared again and invited Thomas to touch His hands and side: "Stop doubting and believe." Thomas answered, "My Lord and my God!" Jesus said, "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed" (John 20:24-29). The story shows that the risen Jesus was real and had a body, and that faith can follow honest doubt.

## The ascension

Jesus appeared to the disciples over forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God. Then, on the Mount of Olives, as they watched, He was lifted up and a cloud hid Him from their sight. Two men in white asked why they stood looking up, and said that Jesus would come back in the same way (Acts 1:9-11).

The ascension means that Jesus' earthly work was completed, that He now reigns with the Father, and that the disciples could now expect the Holy Spirit. The promise of His return gives Christians hope and a reason to live faithfully until He comes.

2.topic: Witnesses to the ends of the earth: Acts 1 and 2
2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain why Jesus told the disciples to wait in Jerusalem (Acts 1:4-8);
2. summarise Peter's sermon at Pentecost and its effect (Acts 2:14-41);
3. describe how the church grew and spread in the early chapters of Acts.

## Materials

Bibles, a map showing Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth, a chart comparing Peter before and after Pentecost.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: why is it easier to speak up when you have a friend beside you? Link it to the Holy Spirit as the helper promised to the disciples.

## Development

1. Read Acts 1:4-8. Draw the three circles on the map: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, the ends of the earth. This is the plan of the book of Acts.
2. Compare Peter's behaviour in Luke 22:54-62 with Acts 2:14. What has changed?
3. Read Acts 2:14-36. Identify the four steps in Peter's argument.
4. Read Acts 2:37-47. List what the new believers did together.
5. Briefly note how persecution later scattered believers and carried the message further (Acts 8:1-4).

## Class activity

Students write a two-column table: "Peter before Pentecost" and "Peter at Pentecost".

## Evaluation

1. What did Jesus say the Holy Spirit would give the disciples?
2. What did Peter tell the crowd to do?

## Assignment

Write a paragraph on how the Holy Spirit changed Peter, using Luke 22 and Acts 2.

reading.title: From waiting to witnessing
reading.content:
# From waiting to witnessing

## Wait in Jerusalem

On the Mount of Olives, shortly before He ascended, Jesus told His disciples not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the gift the Father promised, the Holy Spirit. They asked whether He would now restore the kingdom to Israel. Jesus said that was not for them to know. Instead He said, "You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth" (Acts 1:4-8). This verse gives the plan of the whole book of Acts: the gospel goes out in widening circles, from Jerusalem to the whole world.

The disciples needed to wait because the work was too big for human strength. They also needed the power and courage the Spirit would give.

## A changed Peter

On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter was afraid of a servant girl and denied three times that he knew Jesus. At Pentecost the same Peter stood before thousands in Jerusalem and spoke boldly. What had changed was not Peter's personality but the coming of the Holy Spirit.

## Peter's sermon (Acts 2:14-41)

Peter's argument had four steps.

1. **This is what the prophet Joel promised.** The pouring out of the Spirit, which the crowd saw, was foretold: "In the last days, God says, I will pour out my Spirit on all people."
2. **Jesus was shown to be from God.** God did miracles and wonders through Jesus, which the crowd themselves had seen.
3. **You killed Him, but God raised Him.** Jesus was handed over according to God's plan, but death could not hold Him. Peter quoted David's psalm to show that the Messiah would rise.
4. **God made Him both Lord and Christ.** Peter ended: "Repent and be baptised... and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."

The crowd was cut to the heart. About three thousand believed and were baptised.

## The growing church

The new believers devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. They shared what they had, and the Lord added to their number daily (Acts 2:42-47). Soon the opposition of the authorities scattered believers beyond Jerusalem, and wherever they went they preached the word (Acts 8:1-4). In this way the circles of Acts 1:8 began to widen.

3.topic: Living out family roles: children, parents, workers and employers
3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. apply Ephesians 6:1-4 to situations between children and parents;
2. apply Ephesians 6:5-9 to the relationship between workers and employers, such as house helps and householders;
3. suggest Christian ways of settling disagreements in a Nigerian home.

## Materials

Bibles, situation cards (a child who answers back, a parent who favours one child, a house help who is overworked), chalkboard.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Read out: "Tunde's father calls him to wash the car while his friends are playing football outside." Ask students what each of them would do, and what a Christian should do.

## Development

1. Recall Ephesians 6:1-4 and the reason given: "this is right". Ask students what obedience looks like when you disagree.
2. Read Ephesians 6:5-9. In Paul's day the "slaves" and "masters" were household workers and employers. Ask how the principles apply to a house help today.
3. Discuss "as if you were serving the Lord, not people" and "he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven".
4. Discuss respectful ways of disagreeing: choosing the right time, tone and words.

## Class activity

In groups, students solve two situations from the cards, each in three sentences, quoting a verse.

## Evaluation

1. Why should a worker work well even when the employer is not watching?
2. What should a parent do when a child is disobedient, according to Ephesians 6:4?

## Assignment

Write a short dialogue between a child and a parent who disagree, ending with a Christian solution.

reading.title: Home is where faith is tested
reading.content:
# Home is where faith is tested

It is easier to praise God in church than to obey Him at home. The Bible's teaching on the family is meant for everyday life, and the best test of it is a real situation.

## Children and parents

Paul wrote that children should obey their parents in the Lord because it is right (Ephesians 6:1). This does not mean obedience is always easy. A child who is asked to leave a game to help in the family shop may feel unfairly treated. The Christian choice is to obey cheerfully, and, where there is a real problem, to explain it respectfully at a suitable time, without shouting or sulking. Sometimes parents are unfair. Paul's reply to them is equally clear: do not exasperate your children, but bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4). Favouritism, threats and constant criticism make children angry and discouraged.

## Workers and employers

Paul next speaks to "slaves" and "masters" (Ephesians 6:5-9). Slavery was an accepted part of the Roman world, and Paul does not discuss whether it should exist here, but the principles he gives apply wherever one person works for another. In a Nigerian home, a house help, a driver or a shop assistant is in the position of a worker; the householder or shop owner is the employer.

**What the worker is told:**

- Obey with respect and sincerity of heart, as you would obey Christ.
- Do not work only when you are being watched, to win favour, but do the will of God from the heart.
- Serve wholeheartedly, as if serving the Lord and not only people.

**What the employer is told:**

- Treat your workers in the same way, with fairness and respect.
- Do not threaten them.
- Remember that both of you have the same Master in heaven, who shows no favouritism.

This teaching gives dignity to every worker. A Christian employer cannot treat a house help as less than a person, or leave the wages unpaid, since the Lord will judge the employer too.

## Settling disagreements

Some practical Christian habits for a home are these: speak calmly; listen before answering; choose a suitable time; apologise when you are wrong; and forgive. Paul says everyone in the home has a duty, and all duties are done "as to the Lord".

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain Proverbs 22:1 and say why a good name is valuable;
2. describe Joseph's conduct in Potiphar's house as an example of protecting a good name (Genesis 39:1-20);
3. suggest ways in which a Christian student can uphold the honour of the family.

## Materials

Bibles, newspaper cuttings or a short story about someone whose reputation was lost through dishonesty, flash cards.

Say: "In many Nigerian communities, people say, 'Whose child is this?' before they decide how to treat a young person." Ask what that shows about the importance of a family's name.

## Development

1. Read Proverbs 22:1 and explain "a good name" (reputation and character).
2. Discuss what makes a name good (honesty, kindness, hard work) and what damages it (stealing, cheating, laziness, bad company).
3. Read Genesis 39:1-20. List what Joseph said and did when Potiphar's wife tried to tempt him. Note that he lost his position but kept his integrity.
4. Discuss how Joseph's good name was restored later (Genesis 41:38-41).
5. Connect to the school: exam malpractice, cheating, gossip, disrespect to elders.

## Class activity

Students complete: "A good name is built by... and it can be lost by..." in groups of four.

1. Why did Joseph refuse Potiphar's wife?
2. Give two ways a student can bring honour to his or her family.

reading.title: Better than riches
reading.content:
# Better than riches

"A good name is more desirable than great riches; to be esteemed is better than silver or gold" (Proverbs 22:1).

A **good name** means a good reputation: what people say about you because of how you live. In a Nigerian community, the family name carries weight. When a young man or woman does something, people say, "Whose son is that?" or "Whose daughter?" Good conduct brings honour to the whole family, and shameful conduct brings shame to everyone with that name.

Proverbs teaches that a good name is better than money for two reasons. Money can be lost, stolen or spent, but a good name stays as long as the person lives well. And riches cannot buy trust. Once a trader is known as dishonest, nobody will buy from him, however much he has in the shop.

## What builds a good name

- Honesty in speech, in business and in school work.
- Kindness and respect towards elders and neighbours.
- Hard work and keeping promises.
- Being slow to anger and quick to forgive.
- Choosing friends well.

## What destroys it

- Stealing, cheating and exam malpractice.
- Telling lies and spreading gossip.
- Rudeness and fighting.
- Following bad company.

## Joseph in Potiphar's house (Genesis 39:1-20)

Joseph was sold as a slave in Egypt and served in the house of Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh. He did his work so well that Potiphar put him in charge of the whole household. Potiphar's wife repeatedly tried to tempt Joseph to sin with her. Joseph refused. He said that his master had trusted him with everything except her, and asked, "How then could I do such a wicked thing and sin against God?" One day she caught his cloak, and he ran out of the house, leaving it in her hand. She then lied about him and Joseph was thrown into prison.

Joseph lost his position, but he kept his integrity and his relationship with God. Later God lifted him out of prison and made him governor of Egypt, and his good name was fully restored.

## What we learn

A Christian who protects his or her name will sometimes pay a price in the short term. But doing right honours God and the family. When tempted, we should refuse firmly, and if needed, run from the situation as Joseph did.

## Materials

3. Read Proverbs 1:10-19. List what the sinners say and what Solomon advises: "do not go along with them".

5. Draw up a list of five guidelines for choosing friends.

reading.title: Friends who build, and friends who break
reading.content:
# Friends who build, and friends who break

Friends influence the way we think, speak and act. For this reason the Bible has much to say about whom we should choose as friends.

## David and Jonathan

After David defeated Goliath, he was brought before King Saul. There he met Saul's son, Jonathan. The Bible says that Jonathan became "one in spirit" with David and loved him as himself. They made a covenant, a solemn promise of loyalty. As a sign of it, Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, together with his tunic, his sword, his bow and his belt (1 Samuel 18:1-5). The robe and the sword belonged to a prince. Jonathan, the heir to the throne, was giving them to a shepherd boy, which shows how deep and unselfish his love was.

The friendship was tested. Saul became jealous of David and wanted to kill him. Jonathan could have sided with his father and kept his claim to the throne. Instead he warned David of the danger, and spoke up for him before Saul. At great risk to himself, he arranged a signal with arrows to tell David whether it was safe to return (1 Samuel 20). Before they parted they renewed their promise and wept together.

**Qualities of a true friend:** loyalty, unselfishness, honesty, willingness to protect, and a shared love for God.

## The warning of Proverbs 1:10-19

Solomon warned his son: "My son, if sinful men entice you, do not give in to them." The sinners say, "Come along with us; let's lie in wait for someone's blood, let's ambush the innocent... we will get all sorts of valuable things." Solomon's advice is, "My son, do not go along with them, do not set foot on their paths." Their gain is worthless, since they set a trap for themselves.

This is like peer pressure today. A group may invite a student to join in exam malpractice, to steal, to join a secret cult or to skip class, with promises of excitement or reward. The wise student says no firmly and leaves.

## Guidelines for choosing friends

1. Choose friends who respect God and what is right.
2. Be a good friend yourself.
3. Do not follow a crowd to do wrong.
4. Be loyal, but not to the point of joining wrongdoing.
5. Remember that "bad company corrupts good character" (1 Corinthians 15:33).

3. Read 1 Timothy 2:1-2. Discuss why Christians are told to pray for kings and all in authority.

reading.title: Salt in the community
reading.content:
# Salt in the community

No Christian lives alone. We belong to a family, a school, a church and a community. Jesus said His followers are the salt of the earth and the light of the world (Matthew 5:13-16), which means we are meant to make our communities better.

## Why community relationships matter

- Community members depend on one another for security, health, trade and education.
- Peace in the community makes it possible for people to live and work and for the church to do her work.
- Good conduct towards neighbours is a way of showing love, the second great commandment.

## The Christian and community leaders

In Romans 13:1-7 Paul taught that everyone should submit to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which God has established. Leaders are God's servants to do good, and to punish those who do wrong. He gave Christians four duties:

1. **Obey** the laws of the land, and not rebel against lawful authority.
2. **Pay taxes**, since leaders must be paid to keep the work of government going (Romans 13:6-7).
3. **Give respect and honour** to those to whom it is due.
4. **Live a good life** so that the authorities have no reason to fear or punish us.

In 1 Timothy 2:1-2 Paul asked Christians to make "petitions, prayers, intercession and thanksgiving... for kings and all those in authority, that we may live peaceful and quiet lives in all godliness and holiness." A leader who is prayed for is more likely to rule justly, and a community that prays for its leaders is more likely to enjoy peace.

## Limits

Obedience to leaders is not blind. When the apostles were ordered to stop preaching about Jesus, Peter and John replied, "We must obey God rather than human beings" (Acts 5:29). A Christian will obey a leader unless he commands what God forbids.

## Serving the community

reading.title: One body, many members
reading.content:
# One body, many members

## The body of Christ

Paul wrote to the Christians in Corinth, where there was rivalry over who had the most important gifts. He used the picture of the human body (1 Corinthians 12:12-27).

"Just as a body, though one, has many parts, but all its many parts form one body, so it is with Christ." Every Christian is a member of the body of Christ. Paul made these points:

1. **One body, many parts.** The body does not consist of one part, but of many. The foot cannot say, "Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body." The ear cannot say it is not part of the body because it is not an eye.
2. **Every part is needed.** If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? The parts that seem weaker are indispensable. The eye cannot say to the hand, "I do not need you."
3. **Equal honour.** God has arranged the members so that there is no division, and so that all parts have equal concern for one another.
4. **Shared joy and pain.** "If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honoured, every part rejoices with it."

The lesson is that the church works best when each member uses his or her own gift, respects the gifts of others and cares for fellow members. A choir member, an usher, a teacher and the person who sweeps the church compound are all necessary.

## Fellowship and unity

**Fellowship** means sharing life together: worship, prayer, meals, help in need. **Unity** means being of one mind and purpose though we are different. Paul urged believers to "make every effort to keep the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace" (Ephesians 4:3).

## Service: Jesus washes His disciples' feet (John 13:1-17)

At the Last Supper, Jesus took off His outer clothing, wrapped a towel round His waist, poured water into a basin and began to wash His disciples' feet. This was the work of the lowest servant. Peter protested, but Jesus said, "Unless I wash you, you have no part with me." When He had finished He said, "I have set you an example that you should do as I have done for you." The greatest in the kingdom is the one who serves.

## Ways to practise it today

- Visit the sick and the lonely.
- Welcome new members and visitors.
- Share what we have with those in need.
- Settle disagreements quickly and forgive.
- Offer our gifts and time willingly, however small they seem.

reading.title: Caretakers of the garden, and the cost of the fall
reading.content:
# Caretakers of the garden, and the cost of the fall

## Humans as caretakers

Genesis 1:26-28 says God made human beings in His image and gave them rule over the fish, the birds and every living creature. Genesis 2:15 adds that the Lord God put the man in the Garden of Eden "to work it and take care of it". Rule here does not mean abuse. It means **stewardship**: looking after something that belongs to someone else. The earth belongs to God (Psalm 24:1), and humans are His caretakers.

Today's problems, such as oil spills in the Niger Delta, felling of forests, blocked gutters and refuse dumped in rivers, show what happens when we forget that we are stewards. A Christian should respect and protect the environment as part of obeying God.

## The effects of the fall (Genesis 3:7-24)

When Adam and Eve disobeyed God, every part of their world changed.

1. **Relationship with God.** They were ashamed and hid from God when they heard Him walking in the garden. They were driven out of Eden and could no longer walk with Him as before (3:8, 23-24).
2. **Relationship with each other.** They began to blame each other. Adam said, "The woman you put here with me, she gave me some fruit." The easy harmony between them was damaged (3:12). The woman was told that there would be pain in childbearing, and that tensions would enter the marriage (3:16).
3. **Relationship with the ground.** The ground was cursed because of Adam. He would have to work hard, through painful toil, to grow food, among thorns and thistles (3:17-19). He would return to the dust at last.
4. **Relationship with the serpent.** The serpent was cursed.

## God's mercy

Even so, God did not leave them without hope. He promised that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent's head (3:15), which Christians understand as a first promise of the coming Saviour. He also made garments of animal skins for Adam and Eve and clothed them (3:21). The cherubim and a flaming sword guarded the way to the tree of life, which prevented them from living for ever in a sinful state (3:22-24).

## Lessons

- We are caretakers of God's creation, not its owners.
- Sin damages our relationship with God, with others and with the earth.
- Excuses and blaming others do not remove responsibility.
- God is just, yet merciful.

10.topic: Justice and mercy: Cain's punishment and God's covenant with Noah
10.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain how God dealt with Cain after the murder of Abel, and what this shows about justice and mercy (Genesis 4:8-16);
2. describe God's covenant with Noah after the flood and its sign (Genesis 8:20 to 9:17);
3. draw lessons on obedience and justice from both stories.

## Materials

Bibles, a picture of a rainbow, a chart with columns "What God did" and "What it shows about God".

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: when someone does a terrible wrong, should the punishment be harsh, mild or fair? Take two or three answers and link them to Cain.

## Development

1. Revise Genesis 4:1-8 briefly. Read Genesis 4:9-16, slowly. Note God's question, the curse on Cain and Cain's cry that his punishment is too heavy.
2. Draw out three points: God held Cain responsible, God punished fairly, and God protected Cain with a mark.
3. Revise the flood in outline. Read Genesis 8:20-22 and 9:1-17. Note Noah's altar, God's promise, the command about life and the sign of the rainbow.
4. Draw out how Noah's obedience and God's justice are connected.
5. Link to the way the law protects life today.

## Class activity

Students complete the two-column chart for each story, and one pupil from each group reads a line aloud.

## Evaluation

1. What was the sign of God's covenant with Noah?
2. What did God say about the blood of Abel?

## Assignment

Write a paragraph on how the story of Cain shows that God is both just and merciful.

reading.title: God who judges and God who promises
reading.content:
# God who judges and God who promises

## Cain: judgment with mercy

After Cain killed Abel, God came to him with a question: "Where is your brother Abel?" Cain lied, "I don't know," and asked, "Am I my brother's keeper?" God knew everything. He said, "Your brother's blood cries out to me from the ground." Cain had thought no one saw, but God sees what is done in secret (Genesis 4:9-10).

God then pronounced the punishment. Cain was cursed from the ground that had received his brother's blood. When he farmed, the ground would no longer yield its crops for him. He would be a restless wanderer on the earth (Genesis 4:11-12).

Cain cried that his punishment was more than he could bear and that anyone who found him would kill him. God did not abandon him. God put a **mark** on Cain so that no one who found him would kill him (Genesis 4:13-15). This does not excuse the murder; Cain still had to live with the results of what he did. But it shows that God's justice is accompanied by mercy.

**What it teaches about justice:** God holds every person responsible for what he does. Innocent blood cries out to God. No wrongdoer can hide.

## Noah: the covenant

After the flood, Noah built an altar and offered sacrifices of thanks. God was pleased and said in His heart that He would never again curse the ground because of people, even though human hearts are inclined to evil from childhood (Genesis 8:20-22).

God blessed Noah and his sons and told them to be fruitful and fill the earth. He also gave a command that shows how precious life is: "Whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed; for in the image of God has God made mankind" (Genesis 9:6). Human life is sacred because humans are made in God's image.

Then God made a **covenant**, a binding promise, with Noah, his descendants and every living creature: never again would a flood destroy all life on the earth. As a sign, God set His bow in the clouds, the **rainbow**. Whenever it appears, God said, He would remember His covenant (Genesis 9:8-17).

## Lessons

- Obedience: Noah's careful obedience saved his family. He did all that God commanded (Genesis 6:22).
- Justice: God punishes wrong but protects human life, and requires accountability for the taking of life.
- Mercy and faithfulness: God keeps His promises, and the rainbow reminds us of it.
